lesson.title: Making It Permanent: Soldering Basics and Bench Safety
lesson.summary: Soldering melts a metal alloy onto heated component leads and pads to form a permanent, low resistance joint, turning a validated breadboard prototype into a durable circuit, and it comes with real burn and fume hazards that demand a few consistent safety habits.
lesson.body:
Once a circuit has been built and tested on a breadboard and you are satisfied it behaves the way you intended, the next step in prototyping is often to make that circuit permanent, and soldering is how that is done. Solder is a metal alloy with a relatively low melting point, applied as wire that is typically hollow and filled with a core of flux. A heated soldering iron melts the solder onto a component lead and its pad or wire, and as it cools it solidifies into a solid metal bond that is both a mechanical connection, holding the parts in place, and an electrical one, providing a low resistance path for current, unlike the temporary spring clip contacts inside a breadboard.

Good technique comes down to one central habit: you heat the joint, not the solder. Touch the iron's tip to the component lead and the pad together, hold it there briefly so both are actually hot, and only then feed the solder wire into that heated joint, not onto the iron tip itself. Done correctly, the solder melts, flows around the joint, and is pulled by capillary action into a smooth, shiny, cone shaped fillet. If instead the solder is melted directly on the iron tip and then dropped or smeared onto a lead that was never properly heated, the result is a cold joint: a dull, grainy, weak connection that looks rough rather than shiny, and that can carry unreliable, higher resistance current or fail outright, which matters because a cold joint is a real, if often overlooked, cause of the very kind of intermittent circuit fault discussed later in the chapter on debugging.

Soldering irons are genuinely hot, commonly reaching somewhere in the range of 300 to 400 degrees Celsius at the tip, hot enough to cause a serious burn instantly on contact with skin, so the iron should always sit in its stand when not actively in your hand, never simply set down on the bench, and you should assume the tip and the very end of any freshly soldered joint are dangerously hot until you have had time to confirm otherwise. Molten solder can also flick or drip, so eye protection is a reasonable precaution, and it is worth keeping your face back from the joint rather than leaning in close over it.

The flux core inside solder wire gives off fumes when heated, and those fumes are an airway irritant with continued exposure, so soldering should be done in a well ventilated space, ideally with a fume extractor or fan pulling the smoke away from your face rather than up past it. If you are working with older, leaded solder rather than the lead free alloys common today, washing your hands after handling it is good practice, since lead is a toxin that accumulates with repeated exposure. None of this is meant to make soldering sound exotic or dangerous in the way, say, mains wiring is, it is a routine bench skill practiced safely by hobbyists and professionals every day, but it is a skill with real hazards, and building the habits above from the start is far easier than fixing bad ones later.
